paragraphs: This list is for self-questioning only and does not constitute hiring criteria, an ability score, or a suitability conclusion. The actual work of environmental economists varies greatly: some focus on academic research and government policy assessment, while others focus on environmental economic analysis, cost-benefit assessment, and compliance support at consulting firms; some positions require a master's or doctoral degree and carry responsibility for research design, data scope, and conclusions. Before comparing specific positions, first verify the research object, data sources, review process, and authorship rules.

Verify with one paper-based exercise: given a set of fictional environmental policy options and public data excerpts (emissions, treatment costs, and beneficiary population size), write out within 60 minutes the approach to comparing costs and benefits, key assumptions, data gaps, and the boundaries of the conclusion, and explain which judgments must be reviewed by personnel with the corresponding training and authorization.

Signals worth considering more: willingness to repeatedly verify data sources and statistical scopes, write assumptions and uncertainty clearly, state plainly that "the evidence is insufficient to judge" when it is, and accept that conclusions will be challenged by peers, clients, or approving departments. Signals requiring caution: wanting only to give conclusions without explaining assumptions and limitations, or finding it hard to accept a work rhythm dominated by long-term literature, models, data, and review documents with few immediate results.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute a hiring conclusion, ability score, or academic judgment, nor does it predict employment outcomes.

First judge whether you can sustain data verification, explanation of model assumptions, cost-benefit comparison, and research or report writing, and then judge whether you are willing to work under peer review or client review; verify with the paper exercise and seven-day tasks on this page, not just by the single point of "caring about environmental protection."

The core work of environmental economists is to conduct economic analysis on environmental and natural resource issues: collect and verify data, build or calibrate economic models, assess the costs and benefits of policies and projects, and write assumptions, scopes, and conclusion boundaries into reviewable reports.

U.S. O*NET-SOC 19-3011.01 "Environmental Economists": conduct economic analysis on environmental protection and the use of the natural environment (water, air, land, renewable energy), and apply economic principles and statistical techniques to quantify the costs, benefits, incentives, and impacts of different options.

paragraphs:
Work context｜Environmental economists work mainly on research, data, and policy analysis, completing a work loop around problem definition, data collection, modeling and analysis, conclusion writing, peer review, and communication and release.
Work location｜Office environments at government research departments, universities and research institutes, consulting firms, corporate sustainability departments, and international organizations.
Working conditions｜Mainly desk research and data analysis, requiring long periods of using statistical and modeling software; some positions require field research and public communication.

Main counterparts｜Environmental policies and projects, emission and natural resource data, clients and decision-making departments.
Collaborative relationships｜Requires coordination with economics, statistics, and natural science peers, policy departments, and clients.
Tools and materials｜Statistical and econometric software, databases and geographic data, and literature and regulatory materials.
Institutional basis｜Data and method standards, institutional research and review rules, and client contracts and confidentiality requirements.

Record requirements｜Data sources, versions, assumptions, and calculation processes must be documented so that conclusions can be reviewed.
Safety boundary｜Analysis conclusions are limited by data and assumptions; policy, legal, and compliance judgments must be confirmed by personnel with the corresponding responsibility and authorization.

Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China: environmental surveys and research involving personal data must follow the requirements of legality, least necessity, and informed consent; the specific scope of application is subject to the original text of the law and the interpretation of the competent authorities.

details: Conclusion: most jobs are only partially exposed at the task level, and generative AI is more likely to augment than fully replace; clerical tasks are the most exposed, while the share of highly exposed tasks among managerial and professional occupations is lower.

entries.limitation: Task exposure does not equal actual adoption, productivity, or job changes; economic structures differ greatly across countries.
